power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.77", "P = 0.79", "P = 0.31"), Sentence = c("Across a tenfold range of highest daily dose, from 2 to 20 mg lorazepamequivalent, the fraction of responders reaching remission spanned the whole interval from 0.00 to 1.00 and was uncorrelated with dose (slope on log dose -0.04, P = 0.77; info.title: Catatonia recovery separates two intervention axes that constrain electroconvulsive therapy

author.affiliation:
Department of Neuropsychiatry
								Onda-daini Hospital
								
									Matsudo-shi
									Chiba
									Japan

text.text: A treatment can start a recovery or carry one further, and outcomes alone do not say whether these are actions on the same quantity.

We ask this of a model motivated by catatonia, in which twenty-five inpatients recovered through five capacities in one fixed order and whose two effective treatments have no known dynamical representation.

The model is an evidencecoupled bistable cascade on a dependency chain: each capacity is bistable, the threshold falls as evidence consolidates, and recovery propagates from a root by diffusive coupling.

Two quantities are taken as intervention coordinates, an excursion applied to the root and the coupling between adjacent capacities, with the evidence coordinate closed to input by assumption; we show that they act on disjoint regions of state space.

While every capacity is below threshold, a maximum principle forbids any non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and in either direction, from crossing the switching surface, so an acute conversion requires an excursion.

With the root restored and the downstream chain collapsed, propagation is governed by one exact criterion, the prevailing threshold squared over four, because the first-stage equilibrium condition factorises; the weakest coupling sets where recovery stops, the same discriminant gives the first-stage eigenvalue and the inverse-squareroot passage time through the fold, and the coupling is identifiable from the resting first stage.

Eight falsifiable predictions are separated into consequences of the theorems, predictions needing an added clinical correspondence, and predictions needing a latent quantity measured; exploratory comparisons with published data bear on two of them.
A treatment can act on a recovery in two different ways: it can start a recovery that was not under way, or it can carry further a recovery that has started.
Whether these are two actions on the same quantity or actions on different quantities is not a question that clinical outcomes alone can answer, because both are seen as improvement.

This paper asks it of a dynamical model in which the two can be told apart, a bistable cascade in which capacities are restored one after another along a chain, and in which an intervention may either push the first capacity across its threshold or strengthen the coupling by which a restored capacity pulls the next one along.
The question is motivated by catatonia.

It is a syndrome in which a patient may be unable to move, speak, eat or respond, and two treatments are effective: benzodiazepines, and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) as the established escalation when benzodiazepines fail (Rogers et al. 2023).
text.formatted: It is a syndrome in which a patient may be unable to move, speak, eat or respond, and two treatments are effective: benzodiazepines, and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) as the established escalation when benzodiazepines fail <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Rogers et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Reported response to ECT lies between 59% and 100% across series, is preserved in benzodiazepine non-responders and often follows one or a few treatments (Bush et al. 1996; Sienaert et al. 2014; Lloyd et al. 2020; Pelzer et al. 2018), while chronic partial states respond poorly (Sienaert et al. 2014).
text.formatted: Reported response to ECT lies between 59% and 100% across series, is preserved in benzodiazepine non-responders and often follows one or a few treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bush et al. 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Sienaert et al. 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lloyd et al. 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Pelzer et al. 2018)</ref>, while chronic partial states respond poorly <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Sienaert et al. 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The efficacy of both treatments is established; what is not known is which dynamical action on the recovery process either of them should be represented as, and whether a treatment used both acutely and in a chronic partial state is doing the same thing in the two.

Existing accounts of catatonia are cast in terms of top-down modulation and network dysfunction (Northoff 2002; Hirjak et al. 2024); the present account is about the dynamics of recovery, and asks what an intervention can do to it.

text.text: The model has a specific motivation.

In a series of twenty-five consecutive inpatients managed without ECT, recovery proceeded through five domains, sensory, policy, motivational, fast-volatility and slow-volatility precision, in the same order in every patient, with no inversion (Saito et al. 2026).

text.text: That observation comes from a single centre, and the primary coding was unblinded; a co-author blind to the hypothesis who re-rated every milestone from the nursing records under a pre-registered plan found no inversion of either separable transition, with intraclass correlations on milestone days between 0.71 and 0.90 (Saito et al. 2026).

text.text: Its generality is a matter for prospective testing; here it serves as the motivation for studying recovery as an ordered cascade, and the model is the one derived for that purpose in earlier work, in which the order is the unique linear extension of a dependency chain obtained from structural identifiability (Saito 2026c), the admissible orders of an acyclic dependency graph are its linear extensions (Saito 2026b), and an evidence-coupled bistable cascade on the chain supplies the geometry (Saito 2026a).

text.text: The results below use that model as given, and the reader needs nothing from those papers beyond the equations in Sect. 2, which are restated and proved here where they are used.
The model studied here is a cascade of threshold crossings.
A capacity is one of the five precision domains of Sect.
1.1, represented by a number r in [0, 1] that is zero while the domain is lost and one when it is fully restored.
Each capacity has a stable lost state, a stable restored state and an unstable threshold between them, so on its own it is bistable.
The capacities are arranged along the dependency chain, and a restored capacity pulls the next one towards restoration at a rate proportional to the difference between them, which is the coupling.

The slowest domain is not a capacity but the evidence coordinate: it is the consolidation of the slow-volatility model, it rises only while every other capacity is simultaneously online, and as it rises it lowers the threshold that every capacity must cross.
Recovery is the sequence in which the capacities cross their thresholds, started at the root and propagated down the chain.

The model is that of Saito (2026a), where it was obtained from the dependency structure of Saito (2026c); here it is used as given, and the question asked of it is which of its quantities an intervention can reach and what each can achieve.

The evidence coordinate is excluded from direct input by assumption (Sect.
That choice is a modelling assumption and not a theorem, since the threshold parameters could be moved as well, and Sect.
3.3 shows what it excludes.
We keep the coupling κ as a phenomenological effective coupling defined by the dynamics, its biological implementation unspecified.

The word diffusive carries the argument throughout: coupling that enters as an additive excitatory drive rather than as a difference is not covered by the confinement theorem, and does convert a wholly sub-threshold chain on its own (Sect.
Three results carry the paper.

First, a constraint on starting: while every capacity is below threshold, no non-negative diffusive coupling, on any graph and in either direction, can lift any capacity across it (Theorem 1), so the crossing belongs to the excursion applied to the root and to nothing else (Proposition 3).

Second, a threshold for propagation: for a frozen threshold, with the root held restored and the downstream chain initially collapsed, recovery propagates down the chain if and only if the coupling into each stage exceeds the prevailing threshold squared over four, an exact criterion obtained because the first-stage equilibrium condition factorises (Theorem 2), applied stage by stage so that the weakest coupling decides where recovery stops (Theorem 3).

Third, a change of regime with evidence: because the threshold falls as evidence consolidates, the same coupling can be subcritical early and supercritical later, which divides the coupling axis into immediate propagation, a metastable stall that completes unaided, and confinement, with the boundary between stall and completion given by an explicit formula (Proposition 7).

The two axes carry opposite temporal signatures, a root-driven crossing fast and complete, a coupling-driven escape slow and stepwise, and the same discriminant that sets the propagation threshold sets the first-stage eigenvalue on the partial branch and the passage time through the fold (Proposition 8).

The coupling is recoverable from the resting first stage by an exact estimator (Proposition 9), and the sharp criterion for collapse is not the mirror image of the criterion for recovery (Proposition 6).
The tools are classical: the positively-invariant-region estimate for cooperative systems, the saddle-node bifurcation and its passage time, and geometric singular perturbation theory.
What is added is their arrangement around a question none of them was built for, which quantities an intervention can reach.

The sup-norm invariant region is used to separate two intervention axes on an arbitrary graph rather than to bound a solution; the clamped root makes the first-stage condition factorise, so the critical coupling is a closed-form discriminant rather than the variational pinning criterion of a free front; and an evidence-dependent threshold turns a two-regime coupling axis into three, with the metastable band located by an explicit formula.
The account is falsifiable in eight places, listed in Sect.

11.3 and separated there into consequences of the theorems, which carry conditions of rejection under stated correspondences, clinical predictions that need an added correspondence or a stochastic model not supplied here, and predictions that need a latent quantity measured.
Two exploratory analyses of published aggregate data bear on two of them (Sect.

11.2): across 21 studies of benzodiazepine treatment the depth of recovery among responders is uncorrelated with dose, which the separation of the axes predicts, and none of the ten individually reported patients fell in the intermediate range of improvement.
Neither analysis is a test with power, and they are presented as such.

Section 11.1 states, as a hypothesis and not a derivation, how ECT is represented in the model, and Sect. 12 keeps what is exact apart from what is approximate and names the assumption on which the whole division rests.

Proposition 3 At frozen threshold a and with no incoming coupling, the root obeys the scalar equation dr₀/dt = r₀(1 -r₀)(r₀ -a) + u(t).

For an input supported on [0, τ], the root converges to 1 if r₀(τ) > a and to 0 if r₀(τ) < a, independently of κ and of the state of the other capacities; equivalently, an excursion from full recovery is absorbed if and only if its depth Δ satisfies Δ < Δ_c(Q) = 1 -a(Q).

text.text: Between the two the system stalls after the crossing and then completes spontaneously: residual availability is small but not zero, so Q creeps upward, a(Q) falls, and the branch ceases to exist when a(Q) drops below 2√κ.

Three statements are involved and are kept separate: where the branch ceases to exist, which is algebraic and exact; that a trajectory that stays near the branch reaches that level in finite time, which is a bound under a stated hypothesis; and that the trajectory does stay near the branch and escapes shortly after the fold, which is supported by geometric singular perturbation theory away from the fold and by the numerical integrations through it.

Numerically, escape, detected on a different event function from the fold, followed the predicted fold by 0.003% of the annihilation time at κ = 0.05 and 0.11% at κ = 0.08, and by 0.002% with the wide selector.

text.text: Confinement is a statement about the deterministic field, and the regimes read better as an ordering of timescales than as three fates.
The band is stage-wise as well, and this part is a numerical observation rather than a theorem.

Each stage carries its own locus Q (κ ), but none can cross before its predecessor, so one * ₖ expects stage k to complete when the evidence level first exceeds the running maximum of Q over stages 1 to k; where a stage's own locus lies below that maximum it is released by its * predecessor rather than by its own criterion.

Over five coupling vectors the fifteen completions all sat above that running maximum, by 0 to 0.041, in chain order, and the intervals between them were compressed, 0.004% to 9% of the preceding wait, because a stage coming online multiplies C(r) and accelerates Q. On the evidence coordinate the sequence is a staircase; in time it is often a burst, and late completions should not be evenly spaced.
Two statements about C(r) are used in opposite senses, and both are correct because they refer to different timescales.

The results above are statements about the model, and their clinical use needs a representation, stated as a hypothesis rather than derived.
We take ECT to act as an excursion on the root and, over a course, as an increase of the effective coupling.

A single treatment is a large acute exogenous perturbation, so its representation by u is close to direct; the coupling half is a coarse-grained hypothesis about propagation from one capacity to the next, not an identification with synaptic strength.

Under that representation three clinical regularities follow from the geometry rather than requiring separate accommodations: the response to a graded stimulus is all-or-none (Proposition 3), the shape of the lorazepam challenge (Bush et al. 1996; Sienaert et al. 2014); response after benzodiazepine failure needs only a larger excursion; and conversion can be fast, because beyond the surface the chain converges on the ordinary capacity timescale (Sienaert et al. 2014; Lloyd et al. 2020).

text.text: The two axes are two states in which one treatment cannot be doing the same thing, and the geometry turns that into a conditional.

If the coarse-grained coupling is diffusive, and if the threshold is not itself altered, then no coupling increase converts a wholly sub-threshold configuration (Theorem 1), so an acute conversion requires an excursion-like component.
One half of that conditional can be removed: on the dependency graph the root carries no incoming edge, so no coupling of any form reaches it (Proposition 2).

On the modelled partial branch a partial converse holds: the root is already maximal, the excursion axis saturated and the evidence coordinate closed, so a durable change of the resting profile there is a change of coupling.

Within the architecture, three things other than a change of coupling could take a patient off the branch: an input driving a downstream capacity above its own unstable root, noise, which the shallow barrier admits (Fig. 3b), and spontaneous completion on the band (Proposition 7).

The architecture makes a prediction that published aggregate data can be compared with, though not test with any power.
The excursion axis sets whether a crossing occurs and the coupling axis how far it propagates, so among patients who respond at all the depth of recovery should not depend on the delivered amplitude.

text.text: The account is falsifiable in eight places.

Falsifiability does not require that every internal quantity be measured: a model with latent variables is rejected when an observable consequence it constrains comes out otherwise, and no later choice of the unobserved r , Q or ₖ κ can rescue it.
What it does require is that the condition of rejection be a consequence of the model and not of an assumption added to it.
The eight predictions are therefore sorted by what they rest on.

The first group follows from the theorems under a stated correspondence, milestones with capacities and delivered dose or stimulus with a monotone excursion of the root for (1) and ( 6), and recorded population activity with the coupled variables for (8), and each carries a condition of rejection.

Consequences of the theorems, with their conditions of rejection.

(1) After a single excursion the asymptotic outcome of the root is dichotomous in the value reached (Proposition 3), and the depth to which recovery then propagates is set by coupling, not by the excursion (Theorems 2 and 3).

The observable consequence is that among patients who convert, the eventual depth of recovery does not depend on the delivered amplitude; it is this, and not the improvement score at a fixed early time, that the model constrains, since a finite-time score varies smoothly with the input on either side of the threshold.

Rejected if, with coupling, threshold and downstream initial state held fixed and with the intervention acting only through the root, eventual depth among converters increases with delivered amplitude, dose or charge; an association between dose and depth across patients who differ in coupling, threshold or starting configuration is not by itself a rejection, which is why the comparison of Sect.
11.2 is exploratory.
(6) Arrest, when it occurs, is at a stage of the dependency order with every later stage still down (Theorem 3, with the order of Saito et al. 2026).

(8) The two coupling forms are separated by a sign test rather than by a magnitude: hold two populations at equal activity and ask whether the drive between them vanishes, then lower one and ask whether it reverses; a diffusive coupling does both and an additive drive neither, at any weight.
This needs multi-electrode recordings of the kind that already exist, not a clinical scale, and it is the test on which the whole division rests (Sect.
Rejected, for the diffusive reading, if the drive between equally active populations does not vanish.
Predictions conditional on a correspondence or model not supplied here.

(2) Non-response to a smaller excursion and response to a larger need no patient property beyond amplitude, provided the threshold a(Q) and the mapping from dose to the root excursion do not themselves vary with patient covariates; the model does not exclude that they do, so a covariate that predicts response after conditioning on amplitude is evidence against the model only if it is also shown not to act through the threshold or the mapping.

(4) Within the slow class, frequency of delivery and per-session intensity are interchangeable through their dutyweighted mean (Sect. 8); this is a statement about κ(t), and becomes clinical only under an assumed mapping from the schedule of doses to κ(t), which is not derived here.

(7) The recovered configuration is stable for every coupling, so relapse is a re-crossing of the switching surface by a perturbation exceeding Δ_c(Q) (Sect. 9) and not the decay of a treatment effect; whether relapse hazard then tracks time in the recovered configuration rather than the number of treatments depends on a model of the perturbations, which this paper does not contain. (3), observable half: three kinetic regimes exist on the coupling axis, fast completion, a stall that completes late unaided, and one that does not (Proposition 7); the existence of unaided late completions is the observable consequence, and the distribution of completion times across a population is not constrained, since it depends on the distribution of couplings. text.text: Predictions that need a latent quantity measured. (3), latent half: membership of the three kinetic classes is predicted by the first-stage ratio through a₁²/4 and a₀²/4, which needs an anchored index of the first downstream capacity.
(5) On the branch the resting first-stage ratio is unchanged by an intervention acting on the capacity state and changed by one acting on coupling (Proposition 9), which needs the same index.

Of the two quantities an intervention is allowed to move, with the evidence coordinate closed to input by construction, neither is an alternative to the other: each is powerless exactly where the other is decisive.

The criterion κ_c = a²/4 carries the rest, exact because the first stage factorises, applied stage by stage, and, read as the discriminant whose square root is the firststage rate vanishing at the fold, it fixes the passage time through the fold.

What is exact and what is not should be kept apart: the first stage, the criterion, the locus, the spectrum and the estimator are exact; the stage-wise closed form downstream is an approximation with residual κ r (r ₁ -1), inherited as a bias by the two-ratio inversion.
Every statement about where ₖ ₖ₋ recovery stops is a statement about the collapsed downstream start, since a stage started above its unstable rest point recovers at any coupling (Remark 2).

Three statements of Saito (2026a) are settled here: its unclassified coupling range is classified (Sect. 6), its partial branch continues at every downstream coupling (Proposition 5), and its prediction that consolidation alone cannot remove the branch holds only below a₁²/4 (Proposition 7).

text.text: We are equally explicit about the clinical bridge.
Representing electroconvulsive therapy as an excursion with a coupling component is a hypothesis, asymmetric in its security, and nothing here identifies which physiology realises either axis.
One weakness is better named than left implicit: the whole division rests on the coarse-grained coupling being diffusive.

The one biological observation appealed to here, an increase in co-firing within cell assemblies under stimulation (Moore et al. 2026), does not settle that in either direction, because a change in co-firing, corrected for firing rate or not, reports the coefficient with which one population acts on another, and such a coefficient occupies the same position in the additive form w and in the diffusive form κ.
text.formatted: The one biological observation appealed to here, an increase in co-firing within cell assemblies under stimulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Moore et al. 2026)</ref>, does not settle that in either direction, because a change in co-firing, corrected for firing rate or not, reports the coefficient with which one population acts on another, and such a coefficient occupies the same position in the additive form w and in the diffusive form κ.

text.text: What separates the two is the sign structure of the sink term, which no reported comparison has tested; that is prediction (8).

The two forms also make opposite predictions about the acute state, and prediction (1) separates them there: under diffusive coupling an acute conversion requires an excursion, whereas under an additive drive on a graph with an edge into the root a large enough coupling change converts with no excursion at all.
Several limitations qualify these results.

Theorem 1 holds for arbitrary graphs and unequal thresholds but only for diffusive coupling, and everything after the crossing assumes a forward chain, though κ_c and the branch are unchanged from one stage to twelve.
Which quantities are externally accessible is an assumption.

The identification needs both an anchored index of the first downstream capacity and the threshold prevailing on the branch, no published measure supplies either, and the two state identifications are assumed.

The empirical section is a secondary analysis of published aggregate data: the depth comparison is between studies rather than within them, so it carries the usual ecological caveat and is confounded by chronicity, by underlying diagnosis and by the timing of assessment, while the case-level comparison rests on ten patients from case series and is bounded rather than established by its publication-bias sensitivity.

The dependency order rests empirically on a single series from one centre, in which a hypothesis-blind re-rating reproduced the order without inversion but read the same records as the primary coding, so a bias in what was recorded is not excluded (Saito et al. 2026); and the proportional recovery rule in stroke warns that apparent ordering can arise from ceiling effects and mathematical coupling (Hope et al. 2019); milestone timing in that series did not track peak severity, the rank correlations lying between 0.11 and 0.38 with none significant (Saito et al. 2026).

text.text: The boundaries 0.60, 0.090 and 0.0056 inherit the illustrative set of Saito (2026a), model time is not clinical time, and the waiting time moves by 380 with the regularisation, so timing statements are orderings.

The evidence coordinate is closed to external input by construction, and the two quantities an intervention can move act on disjoint regions, so a treatment used both acutely and in the chronic partial state cannot be doing the same thing in each.
Electroconvulsive therapy is the case in point.

Acutely it is predicted to act as an excursion on the root, u, because no nonnegative diffusive coupling carries a wholly sub-threshold configuration across the switching surface, on any graph and in either direction, and because the root of the dependency graph has no incoming edge for any coupling to use.

On the chronic partial branch it is predicted to act as an increase of the effective coupling, κ, because there the root is already maximal, the excursion axis saturated and the evidence coordinate closed.

Between the two, one exact criterion, a(Q)²/4, applied stage by stage, sets how far recovery reaches and when each stage completes, and gives the first-stage eigenvalue and the inverse-square-root passage time through the fold.

Both halves of the prediction are conditional on the coupling form and on identifying the two presentations with the two configurations, neither shown here, and the resting first-stage ratio is what would decide them.

Published aggregate data are so far consistent with both: the depth of recovery is uncorrelated with dose, and no individually reported patient fell in the intermediate range of improvement, though neither comparison has the power to decide.
The division does not rest on the disorder, but it does rest on the model class.

Within the class of Sect. 2, bistable capacities on a dependency chain, non-negative diffusive coupling, a threshold lowered by an evidence coordinate that is closed to input, and interventions restricted to the root excursion and the coupling, the maximum principle of Theorem 1 holds on any graph, and the criterion a²/4 is a property of a clamped bistable stage rather than of the five precision domains; the three coupling regimes follow when, in addition, the threshold ranges over [a₁, a₀] under the evidence dynamics of (2).

text.text: What the paper adds to the mathematical description of staged recovery is therefore not a law for every cascade but an analytic separation, within an explicit model class, of the action that starts a recovery from the action that propagates it: from a wholly sub-threshold configuration the root excursion is the only action that produces a crossing, and on the partial branch, where the root is saturated and the evidence coordinate closed, a change of coupling is the only action that moves the resting profile.
A staged recovery for which the same class and the same three conditions can be argued is a candidate for the same separation, and nothing more is claimed for it here.

The escape time above the critical coupling diverges as a power of the excess with exponent one half (Sect. 7 of the main text), and two separate effects push a fitted exponent away from that value.

The first is pre-asymptotic curvature: at any finite excess the fit still contains the approach to the asymptote, so it exceeds one half over a wide range and falls towards one half as the excess is reduced.

The second is feedback through the evidence coordinate: while the system waits on the branch, Q rises, a(Q) falls and the critical coupling moves, so the excess against which the fit is taken is not the excess the system experiences.
The first effect is present in the capacity subsystem, which has no evidence channel; the second exists only at a positive evidence rate.
The control separates them by a single change.

The full five-dimensional sweep is repeated with ε set to zero and everything else, including the six evidence levels, the starting point at half the critical coupling for the prevailing threshold, the excess grid and the solver settings, held fixed.

With the evidence channel off the capacity block depends on the evidence level only through the constant a, and the excess is measured in units of the corresponding κ_c; the asymptotic exponent is then one half at every level, but an exponent fitted over a finite range of excess may still differ between levels, because the scaled first-stage equation retains a dependence on a (below).
Table S1 Exponents of the full system with the evidence channel on and off.

With the channel off the six levels agree to within 0.007 in the full-range exponent (0.570 to 0.577) and to within 0.005 in the small-excess exponent (0.527 to 0.532), across a threshold range of a factor of four, against a spread of 0.146 in the same column with the channel on.

Switching the channel off therefore removes most of the spread between levels; the small spread that remains is not analysed further, and since the first-stage equation in scaled variables, dy/dτ = (1 -ay)(y² -y + K) with r₁ = ay, κ = a²K and τ = at, retains a dependence on a, a finite-range exponent is not expected to be identical across thresholds even where the asymptotic exponent is one half in each case.

At Q₀ = 1 the two sweeps agree to every digit reported, because z > 0 on the branch makes the only inflow term proportional to 1 -Q, which vanishes there, so the evidence coordinate is stationary and ε cannot act.

text.text: Continuing the control to smaller excess shows the approach to the asymptote over the range computed.

At Q₀ = 0.5 the local slope between consecutive excesses is 0.512 at 3.2 × 10 ³, ⁻ 0.508 at 1.4 × 10 ³, 0.505 at 7.1 × 10 ⁴ and 0.504 at 3.2 × 10 ⁴; at Q₀ = 0 the same sequence ⁻ ⁻ ⁻ is 0.510, 0.507, 0.505 and 0.503.
Both approach one half from above at the two thresholds examined, which differ by a factor of 1.23.
One alternative explanation is excluded arithmetically rather than numerically.
Every sweep starts on the exact partial branch at κ = κ_c/2, and the first stage there is r₁ = a(1 -1/√2)/2, while the branch remnant at κ_c is r₁ = a/2.
The ratio is 1 -1/√2 = 0.2929 at every threshold, since a cancels.

The starting point is therefore the same fraction of the way to the fold at every evidence level, so a difference in the normalised initial position does not account for a spread across levels; a difference in the dynamics through the threshold a is not excluded by this argument.
On the intermediate band (Proposition 7 of the main text) the time to reach Q (κ) is set by ε * C(r) and by the selector scale.

In the full-system integrations it ranges from 8.8 × 10⁵ time units at κ = 0.08 with the narrow selector (s = 0.01) to 3.4 × 10⁸ at the same coupling with the wide one (s = 1), a factor of 380, and to 4.9 × 10⁷ at κ = 0.05 with the narrow selector.
Below a₁²/4 the locus does not exist and no waiting time is defined.

The existence of the band, its two boundaries a₁²/4 and a₀²/4, the locus Q (κ) and the ordering of the fold and the escape * follow from the geometry and are reported as results in the main text; the absolute waiting time is not a prediction, since it inherits the evidence rate and the regularisation of Saito (2026a) and varies by more than two orders of magnitude between the two selector scales.
No clinical timescale is claimed from it.

Except where stated, analyses were run on the capacity subsystem (1) with the threshold held at a fixed value.

The equilibria of that subsystem are exact objects; as a description of the full system over the time windows used, holding the threshold fixed is an approximation, accurate to below every reported digit for the equilibrium quantities on the partial branch, where the joint availability that drives the evidence coordinate is of order 10 ¹ so that Q moves by less ⁻ ⁰ than 10 ⁹ over an escape interval (Sect. 6), while the escape times near the fold were ⁻ measured in the full system as well (Appendix A.7); it is conservative from a collapsed state, where the root lies below threshold and the evidence channel only attenuates.
The full fivedimensional system (1)-(2) was used for the intermediate-regime integration and for the confirmatory exponent measurement, with the illustrative parameters of Sect.
2.1 throughout.
Integration used an adaptive stiff solver with relative tolerance 10 ¹ and absolute tolerance ⁻ ⁰ 10 ¹³, with event detection for crossings.

One hundred systems were drawn from each of four graph families, feed-forward chains, symmetric graphs, purely reverse chains and general directed graphs, on three to six nodes, with weights drawn from a mixture placing mass at zero, 0.5, 3 and 30 times a uniform draw on (0, 1].

The same mixture was used for every family, restricted to the sub-diagonal for feedforward chains, symmetrised for symmetric graphs and transposed into the strict upper triangle for purely reverse chains, so no family was given a narrower weight distribution than another.

Every capacity was initialised below a₀ and the system integrated with no external input; recorded quantities were whether any capacity reached the threshold and the largest increase of max r over its initial value.
Separately, in the forward chain, root trajectories ₖ ₖ from the same sub-threshold initial condition were computed at κ = 0.6, 3.0 and 30.0 on a common dense grid and compared pointwise.
The reverse-coupling counterexample used a bidirectional chain from r = (0.30, 0.90, 0.90, 0.90), at forward weight 0.01 with reverse weight 0.10 and with reverse coupling alone.
A further 200 general directed graphs were drawn with a threshold per node from the uniform distribution on [a₁, a₀] and every capacity initialised below the smallest of them.

3.2) from the same start and from the fully collapsed corner, at weights from 0.01 to 100 and with both forms of S, bracketing the weight at which each stage converts.
The collapse criterion (Proposition 6) was obtained by holding the root at zero and bisecting the coupling at which the first stage loses its high equilibrium, at both threshold levels.
Pulses were applied as u(t) = A on [0, τ] and zero afterwards, from the collapsed chain at Q = 0, at durations τ = 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 and 5.
For each duration the critical amplitude was bracketed by bisection, and outcomes recorded at 0.8, 0.99, 1.01 and 1.2 times it together with the root value reached at the end of the pulse.

A separate sweep set the root directly to a value v with no input, over a grid spanning a₀ and refined near it; v = a₀ lies on the invariant surface and was excluded from the grid rather than integrated.
The transition was located by bracketed root-finding at three coupling values; the located boundary agrees with a₀ to twelve digits, which is a check on the solver.
The propagation experiment of Sect. 4 placed the root at 0.61 with the rest at zero and integrated to 3 × 10⁴ at κ = 0.6, 0.2, 0.095, 0.085, 0.05 and 0.01.
The first stage was taken from the factorised quadratic (4), which is exact.

Each downstream stage was obtained as the low root of its cubic, bracketed on (0, a) by Proposition 5 and solved to machine precision; the residual of the vector field at that profile was below 10 ¹⁸, ⁻ and a perturbation of 10 ⁴ in every downstream capacity returned to it.
The stage-wise closed ⁻ form was retained only to quantify its departure, reported as a relative error against the exact profile and against the analytic residual of Proposition 4.
The propagation boundary was located by bracketed root-finding on the coupling at which a supracritical excursion reaches the distal capacity.

In the full system the fold was located as a separate non-terminal event at a(Q)² -4κ = 0; because that event function is the discriminant from which the locus ( 7) is derived, the agreement it reports is a check on the solver rather than a test of the formula, and the independent comparison is with the escape event, detected on r₃ -a(Q) = 0.

text.text: Identification was evaluated on the exact equilibrium, for the first-stage estimator (11) and for the closedform two-ratio inversion, without noise and then under multiplicative lognormal noise of coefficient of variation 1%, 5% and 10%, two thousand draws per level, reporting medians and interquartile ranges.

For unequal coupling each stage was given its own κ , and the boundary of a single stage was ₖ bracketed by bisection on that stage with the others held at 1.0, from the same supracritical excursion used for the equal-coupling boundary.
The constants of Lemma 1 were evaluated on a grid of 20001 points on [0, 0.9] and the bound on the crossing time checked against the integrated comparison equation at four couplings above a₀²/4.

Arrest depth was read from seven coupling vectors as the number of downstream capacities above 0.5 at the end of the integration, and compared with the index of the first stage whose coupling does not exceed a(Q)²/4.

Existence of the branch was tested at κ₁ = 0.005625 and 0.00563 with downstream couplings spanning 10 ⁴ to 30, and the critical coupling was located by bisection to 10 ¹⁴ at ⁻ ⁻ chain lengths from one stage to twelve.
The spectrum was taken as the diagonal of the capacity Jacobian on the exact branch at three thresholds and ten couplings per threshold and compared with (8).

For the noise runs the capacity block was integrated by Euler-Maruyama with additive Wiener increments of standard deviation σ on each capacity, step 0.05, the root held at 1, 500 paths per σ and a horizon of 2 × 10⁴; escape was the first stage crossing its own unstable root, and the barrier was computed from the potential of the first-stage field.
The coupling was modulated as a rectangular wave between a base value of 0.003 and an elevated value, with duty fraction f, starting from the exact partial branch.
Escape was scored as the most distal capacity crossing the unstable root of its own bistable law.
For the criterion grid the period was one fiftieth of the static escape time at a duty-weighted mean of 1.2 κ_c.

For the period sweep the duty fraction and elevated value were fixed so that the dutyweighted mean equalled 1.2 κ_c, and the period was varied from 10 ³ to 5 times that static ⁻ escape time; runs in which the escape completed inside the first elevated phase were flagged, since the ratio saturates there and successive points are not independent.
Escape times were recorded at excesses from 10 ⁵ to 0.8 above the critical coupling.
The ⁻ local slope was computed between consecutive excesses, and regressions were also taken over the full range and restricted to excesses below 5%.
Reported escape times are for the most distal capacity crossing the unstable root of its own law, which is the definition of the escape time and not the completion of recovery.

The measurement was repeated in the full system at Q = 0, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.99 and 1, in each case starting from the exact partial branch at half the critical coupling for the prevailing threshold, and then repeated again with the evidence rate set to zero and every other setting left unchanged; that control isolates the contribution of evidence feedback (Online Resource 1, Sect. 1), and it was extended to an excess of 2 × 10 ⁴ ⁻ at Q = 0 and Q = 0.5 to locate the asymptote.
The fraction of the escape interval showing no appreciable change was computed at rate thresholds from 0.5% to 20% of the maximum rate and is reported as a range rather than a single value.

text.text: The hypothesis that the trajectory stays near the branch, with every downstream * capacity bounded below by c₀, is what geometric singular perturbation theory supplies away from the fold (Proposition 8; Fenichel 1979): on the branch all capacities are positive (Proposition 5) and the branch is normally hyperbolic (Proposition 8), so for ε small the trajectory tracks it to O(ε) on compact evidence intervals bounded away from Q (κ).
The * passage through the fold itself is not covered by that estimate; it is observed numerically.
Appendix A.10). (11) needs one stage and no assumption about the others.This is what makes the two axes distinguishable in practice.
An intervention acting only on the capacity state leaves the resting profile of a partial branch unchanged; one acting on coupling moves it, by a calculable amount, without the patient recovering.

The estimator uses r₁ itself and not a monotone transform, so it needs an index of the first downstream capacity anchored at zero for complete failure and at one for the fully recovered level in the same patient, and Saito (2026c) says why no scale supplies it: a cross-sectional reading does not separate the first two downstream capacities, which recovery timing separates.

It also needs the threshold prevailing on the branch, a(Q), which an acute challenge does not read, since a graded challenge probes the collapsed configuration and estimates a₀, whereas the branch sits at consolidated evidence, and the two differ fourfold; (12) would supply it only under equal coupling and with r₂ measured to better than one per cent.
At κ = 0.003 the estimator (11) returns 2.19 times the true coupling if a = 0.30 is used and 4.56 times it at a₀, against 12% for a 10% error in the correct threshold.
The coupling is therefore structurally identifiable and not operationally measurable.

Association with dose was tested by least-squares regression on log dose and by Spearman rank correlation, and the count in the partial window by an exact binomial test.
